name: Antioquia
summary:
By a wide margin the most lethal department for LGBTIQ+ people in Colombia. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report records 45 of the country's 270 LGBTIQ+ killings in Antioquia, and its director names the department "one of the most dangerous for LGBTIQ+ people in Colombia." Three of those deaths occurred in the single municipality of Bello. The emblematic case is Sara Millerey González Borja, 32, a trans woman recycler brutally beaten and thrown into the Quebrada La García on 4 April 2025 while onlookers filmed her struggling without intervening; her death triggered a national transfeminicide alert and sits within a series of at least 13 trans-women murders reported in 2025.

No institutional-protection finding appears for Antioquia in the monitoring reports; the framing is "prejudice, violence and impunity." The killing mechanism is patterned: motorcycle-borne attackers, public streets, trans women in or adjacent to sex work, suspects at large weeks later.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Antioquia falls approximately 0.19 lower, justified by the extreme concentration of lethality (16.7% of all national killings), the absence of any state-implicated positive response, and the explicit "most dangerous" designation from Colombia's principal monitoring NGO. Versus Bogotá (~0.46), Antioquia is further below because Bogotá's risk includes police violence but also the district's published studies and mayoral intervention, whereas Antioquia shows neither legal exposure nor institutional counterweight.

name: Bogota Capital District
summary:
Bogotá combines Colombia's best-documented trans community and district-level services with a repeated police-violence pattern in the Santa Fe/Los Mártires tolerance zone. The Red Comunitaria Trans reported that at 3:50 a.m. on calle 22 con Caracas, metropolitan police shouted at, baton-struck and shot at trans sex workers; the district mayor's office took up the case. A night of 2 January 2026 saw two trans women beaten to death within hours—"Catia," 24, in Engativá (suspect sought a week later) and a 20-year-old in Florida Blanca—treated by Caribe Afirmativo as part of the national series. In December 2023, trans activist Roxanna Delgado Trujillo was found dead; El Espectador framed the case as "recurring mechanisms in crimes against trans women," not an isolated incident.

District "mega-operativos" in the same area—200+ officials in San Bernardo (April 2025) and more than 1,200 uniformed officers in Santa Fe (January 2026)—conduct registration, background checks and migrant control with arrests, placing a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor in the path of institutional sweeps. The Bogotá Mayor's Office law journal carries its own study of violence in the tolerance zone.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Bogotá sits approximately 0.06 lower: the police-violation pattern and killing cluster are state-implicated and recurring, offsetting the district's comparative institutional infrastructure. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Bogotá is notably higher because, despite the Jan 2026 homicides and mega-operativos, the district publishes violence studies, its mayor's office intervenes in police-complaint cases, and trans-community services are more developed than anywhere else in Colombia.

name: Atlántico
summary:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department," situating Barranquilla within the national territorial-expansion finding rather than treating it as an undifferentiated count. Barranquilla is the Caribbean-coast hub for trans sex work and the city where the NGO's documentation base operates, giving it both elevated exposure and visibility in monitoring data. The department appears explicitly in the 270-victim national total.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Atlántico falls approximately 0.09 lower, justified by the NGO's named escalation warning (not merely inclusion in aggregate counts, but a specific "increase" call-out) and the structural role of Barranquilla's trans sex-work corridor. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Atlántico is higher: its violence is a rising trend flagged by Caribe Afirmativo rather than the decade-deep, impunity-saturated lethality concentration that makes Antioquia "one of the most dangerous" in Colombia. Versus Bolívar (0.44), Atlántico sits marginally lower because its finding is a forward-looking escalation warning tied to a specific urban hub, whereas Bolívar's deviation rests on one targeted killing of a named community leader.

name: Bolívar
summary:
The murder of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who campaigned with the "No Es Hora De Callar" movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of 500+ survivors of sexual violence, is documented in Bolívar on 22 May 2025. El Tiempo's data-journalism work on the gap between official Fiscalía and NGO (Caribe Afirmativo/Defensoría) figures names her case specifically. Bolívar appears within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged by Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 territorial-expansion finding, where state response is weakest.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Bolívar sits approximately 0.08 lower: the killing is a named, targeted murder of a community leader (not an undifferentiated count), and the department falls within the "territorial expansion" zone where the monitoring body documents insufficient state protection. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Bolívar is substantially higher because it carries one specific high-profile homicide rather than the 45-of-270 structural concentration and multi-case impunity pattern defining Antioquia. Versus Atlántico (0.43), Bolívar is marginally above: its evidence is a single named killing within an aggregate warning, whereas Atlántico carries a forward-looking escalation call-out tied to a larger trans sex-work hub.
